description: The Greeks table gives every Greek in closed form -- delta N(d+) for a call and N(d+)-1 for a put, gamma N'(d+)/(S sigma sqrt(T-t)), vega S N'(d+) sqrt(T-t), and theta and rho for both -- and not one of them was extracted. Three units discuss what the Greeks are, how they are scaled and why gamma and vega match across calls and puts, while the actual formulas, which are the reason the section exists, were skipped. The table is asset tbl-src-black-scholes-model-fa32a5b3-0001 and its cells are citable by row and column.
excerpt: The Greeks for Black–Scholes are given in closed form below. They can be obtained by differentiation of the Black–Scholes formula.

description: The third asset assumption -- that the stock pays no dividend -- is absent, though the other two (constant risk-free rate, geometric Brownian motion) were both extracted. It is the assumption the whole dividend-extension section exists to relax, so its absence breaks the link between the base model and its extensions.
excerpt: The stock does not pay a dividend.

description: Delta is singled out as the most important Greek because it usually carries the largest risk, and the daily practice that follows from this -- traders zeroing their delta at the end of the day when not speculating on market direction -- is not represented.
excerpt: Delta is the most important Greek since this usually confers the largest risk.

description: Two named approximations for American options are absent: Barone-Adesi and Whaley, which splits the SDE into the European value plus the early-exercise premium and solves a quadratic for the latter, and Bjerksund and Stensland, which uses a trigger-price exercise strategy and is computationally inexpensive and fast. The extraction says no closed form exists in general but names none of what practitioners use instead.
excerpt: Barone-Adesi and Whaley[29] is a further approximation formula.

description: The scope of the model's extensions is stated and not captured: variable but deterministic rates and volatilities are accommodated, closed-form solutions survive when the dividend is a known proportion of the stock price, and American options and known cash dividends are the harder cases.
excerpt: The above model can be extended for variable (but deterministic) rates and volatilities.

description: The implied-volatility-surface use of the model is missing: solving for volatility across durations and strikes constructs the surface, and this amounts to a coordinate transformation from the price domain to the volatility domain. One unit mentions reversibility in passing; the mechanism is not recorded.
excerpt: Explicit modeling: this feature means that, rather than assuming a volatility a priori and computing prices from it, one can use the model to solve for volatility, which gives the implied volatility of an option at given prices, durations and exercise prices.

description: The market-assumptions unit carries four assumptions that are independently true or false and independently relaxable -- no arbitrage, unlimited fractional borrowing and lending, unlimited fractional trading including short selling, and no transaction costs.
